388.t: The first Gibson jazz party with Ralph Sutton and Teddy Wilson
388.s: Gibson hires Ralph Sutton, Cutty Cutshall, Wild Bill Davison, Edmund Hall and Jack Lesberg plus Teddy Wilson's trio for an invitation-only Labor Day party, with the band traveling to Aspen by bus.
388.q: ... the intermission piano player at Condon's for several years was Ralph Sutton, and he just loved Ralph. So he hired Ralph to be our piano player at that first party -- so that was the band. Ralph Sutton, Cutty Cutshall, Wild Bill Davis son, Edmund Hall, Jack Lesberg on bass. Then he hired one…

388.t: Growth of Gibson's parties: the Jerome Hotel in Aspen
388.s: The second Aspen party outgrew its dining room; Leeman suggested adding the Lawson-Haggart band, and he has kept Gibson's handwritten set lists since 1962.
388.ch: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
388.q: Those are enough accolades for the present, and now I will get on with some more notes. I'd like to do a fast resume of the Richard Gibson, the Dick Gibson parties that he started in '62 in Aspen. We covered some of that, and the first band which was his favorite -- Condon band, and with Teddy…

388.t: Gibson parties move to Vail and the Broadmoor Hotel
388.s: The parties moved to Vail, back to Aspen, and then to the Broadmoor in Colorado Springs, growing to hundreds of guests and 67 musicians.
388.ch: Honors, Gibson and Dorsey late years
388.q: But we don't have time on these tapes to go through all the personnel. The fourth year or so, he decided for a change of scenery, and the guest list was growing larger and larger, and in fact, the parties were, as I say, the guest list was larger, and the party gained prominence around the country…

388.t: Odessa party musicians: Flip Phillips, Buddy Tate, Dave McKenna and Teddy Wilson
388.s: Leeman lists the bassists, trumpeters, trombonists, reed players, pianists and vibes at a recent party and praises Teddy Wilson's breakneck tempos.
388.q: Oh, yes, I have those sets of the different jazz stars performing also on file. And I would love to furnish those also to the Institute files for the research and digests.

388.t: How the Odessa jazz party works
388.s: Leeman describes the six-day invitation-only party held in west Texas, with 20 to 25 players, four-hour nights and lavish hospitality from wealthy sponsors.
388.q: I believe their first party was in 1966. Their party is a beautiful, intimate and it's six days long, instead of the three day short parties of other people -- that other people hold -- and it is held in the unique Inn of the Golden West Hotel, and our wives, girlfriends, what have you, are always…

388.t: Odessa jazz party founded by Dr. Fulcher
388.s: Leeman is hired again for Gibson's 1979 party, his 17th, then explains how Dr. Jim Fulcher founded the invitation-only Odessa, Texas jazz party.
388.q: I'm going to attempt to do a couple of like -- I have to skipover so much and not get deeply into the subject, but I want to get into the subject of some of the jazz parties that are spin offs from the Gibson parties, and I'm gonna start, as Milt Hinton will agree with me, I'm sure -- the next big…

388.t: Midland and Manassas parties as spin-offs of Gibson's
388.s: Max Christianson starts a Midland party in 1977 with some Odessa players, and Leeman notes other offshoots in New Jersey and Manassas, Virginia.
388.q: Another insert on the jazz parties, was one of our fans in the Odessa parties was a gentleman called Max Christianson from Midland, Texas -- of course, that's only 30 minutes away, about 30 or 40 miles from Odessa.

388.t: Dick Gibson as jazz patron and philanthropist
388.s: Hinton and Leeman credit Dick Gibson for his private jazz parties in Colorado, which Leeman has played every year, and for helping down-and-out musicians and reviving Joe Venuti.
388.q: And helping me personally, among other things -- not only promoting jazz, but he went for a load of money and kept up his, and didn't let down on it.

115.t: Jack Lesberg's invitation to Dick Gibson's party
115.s: Jack Lesberg mentioned a rich man's yearly party in Colorado and a year later arranged for Gus to be paid $400 to attend.
115.ch: World's Greatest Jazz Band and Denver
115.q: Oh, yeah, that's right. And Jack came in the club there. I was playing there, with Zoot and Al Cohen. And so I went over and spoke to him during intermission, like I came over and I said, 'Hey, Jack, where have you been? I haven't seen you in a long time,' like that.

115.s: Gus describes arriving in Vail, playing with Teddy Wilson, Milt Hinton and others, and being asked back.
115.ch: World's Greatest Jazz Band and Denver
115.q: He called me after Jack got finished talking. He called me later, and he told me the same thing Jack had just told me, see.

115.t: The tuba ensemble at the party
115.s: He and Carl Fontana did not play together; a tuba ensemble played Basie arrangements.
115.ch: World's Greatest Jazz Band and Denver
115.q: Yes, yes. And Ray Brown's wife was there. And I said, 'I wonder what's the surprise group this time?' See, the year before that, it was the Japanese girls.

115.s: Players see a slip each day; Gibson pays their way.
115.ch: World's Greatest Jazz Band and Denver
115.q: He's paying their way here, from over in Hawaii and all across like that.

I played with George. And I really enjoyed it, you know. It was fun. It was a fun thing. It got to cooking…

87.t: Why he loves Dick Gibson's jazz party
87.s: He praises the party's closeness and organization, with Gibson improvising set combinations such as Faddis and Eubie Blake.
87.q: Well, it's a lot of -- it's different from probably any of those things you'll ever see. It's altogether different, you know. You're so close to the guys because, you know, it's one of those things. And, you know, you don't need no guards or nothing backstage or nothing. You know, everybody's just…

235.t: Jazz at Noon in New York three years earlier
235.s: His only New York date in years was a Jazz at Noon Friday session for Les Leiber with amateur businessmen players.
235.q: Yeah, I did that for him. That was very nice and that was the only thing I've done in the last six or seven years in New York, or eight years. Yeah.

235.t: Returning to the Tin Palace and the West End in 1979
235.s: He found audiences wanting romantic, basic music; he played the Tin Palace with John Hicks, Walter Booker and Jimmy Cobb and the West End, where old friends like Beverly Peer came.
235.q: : Well, what I noticed this time was that, you know, the wheel always turns, the wheel never stops turning, but people want to go back to basic things and they want to go back to soul and people, I mean they want a little more romantic music, mainly, that's what they want. They want something that…

155.t: How Budd came to attend Dick Gibson's jazz parties
155.s: From Cliff Leeman and Peanuts Hucko to the 1969 invitation, and meeting Gibson's wife again.
155.q: Yes, I did. The first one was at the Gibson one, which started — I never heard of these things but I read about them in the jazz magazines. One time at Eddie Condon’s place, Cliff Lehman, who was a drummer in those days with the bunch around Condon’s, and he said “you like music so much, there’s a…

132.t: Collecting records and meeting musicians at Dick Gibson's jazz parties
132.s: He met musicians through Gibson's parties from the early 1960s and values their loyal friendship.
132.ch: Jazz parties, Metropole and San Diego
132.q: Yeah, somewhat. But mostly after the law school and so on, that’s when I really picked up on it. Because while I was in the Navy and here I didn’t have any time to do it. But I did then, yes.

466.t: Jazz parties as a social oasis
466.s: Jazz parties mean little playing but reunions with old friends like Kenny Davern and meeting Joe Cohn.
466.q: The fun of it for me — you know there’s not much playing to do. It’s mostly waiting around to play. And so from that point of view they are kind of frustrating. You leave four days or three days later not having hardly played more than forty minutes. There’s ten piano players here, and only one of…

562.t: Promoting jazz parties in Irvine and elsewhere
562.s: She talks about the Labor Day mainstream jazz party she is involved in and other festivals.
562.q: Every year at the Labor Day Weekend, and the roster just came out in the press today, so it’s a wonderful jazz party, it’s one of the only mainstream jazz parties.

695.t: Jazz festival and scholarship honoring her 80th birthday
695.s: Jarvis describes the November festival in her honor, organized by Jazz Music Education, Inc., and the Jane Jarvis Jazz Piano Scholarship aimed at building jazz audiences among young people.

215.t: Jazz parties in Odessa and Denver

368.s: He explains how the Whitefish and Missoula festivals began.

66.t: Cardinal Wright and the Pittsburgh jazz festival

383.s: Wilson likes the parties as reunions of old friends even though sets can come very late.

566.t: Favourite rooms and the Johns Manville jazz parties in Denver
566.s: She liked the Hyatt hotels in New Orleans and Indianapolis. Johns Manville's president Mr. Goodwin held annual jazz parties in Denver where she got a huge suite, a limousine and catered parties.
566.ch: Jazz at the Philharmonic and life on the road
566.q: It was just like living like a millionaire because I had a great big two bedroom, two bathroom suite by myself with a living room, dining room, kitchen and bar. That was just for me.

386.t: Phil Schaap and the West End
386.s: He returns to playing at the West End in 1975.
386.q: come over to the West End. That's another re-entry into the music world. I went back into it again, after, you know, being involved in the problems in Harlem. And I went back to the West End and I predicted that that place would become, you know, one of the real musical arenas in America, you know,…

You know, all around (inaudible). After…
